Cognitive Biases in Performance Evaluations
abs: Performance evaluations are a central component in the administration of public organizations. The predominant model of how both public managers and citizens evaluate performance suggests that satisfaction judgments about performance are based on a comparison of performance to some adapted standard like expectations or goals. However, in a number of experiments we show that perceptions of performance and satisfaction are formed in ways that are not so consistent and better explained by an intuitive mode of thinking. The results question the validity of citizen satisfaction as a measure of performance but also raise more general questions about how performance information is processed by citizens and public managers. Suggestions for a more adequate theory of the relationship between performance and satisfaction and implications for the use of performance information in public organizations are presented and discussed.

t: The State, the Economy, and the Regions: Theories of Preference Formation in Times of Crisis
abs: As a response to the sovereign debt crisis, European states have carried out various reforms. In this process, they have sought to readjust the balance between free-market logics and the role of government. These reforms are often implemented—and sometimes co-decided—by regional administrations. Little is known, however, about the governance preferences of the élite officials directing these administrations. This is paradoxical since regional administrations play a crucial role in the recovery strategies of European states. What are the views of regional administrative élites on the regulation of the economy, the role of government, and that of the free market? Are these views related to (1) early-life socialization, (2) educational pathways, (3) professional interests, or (4) the capacity of their own administration? To answer these questions, we assembled a unique dataset by interviewing 742 administrative élites from 63 regions and 11 countries. We find some supporting evidence for all four explanations. However, while the individual characteristics of these élites matter, contextual factors seem to matter more. В ответ на кризис суверенного долга, европейские государства провели различные реформы. В этом процессе, они стремились скорректировать баланс между логикой свободного рынка и ролью правительства. Эти реформы часто реализуются, а иногда совместно решаются, региональными администрациями. Мало что известно, однако, о предпочтениях чиновников верхнего элитного эшелона управляющих этими администрациями. Это парадоксально, поскольку региональные администрации играют ключевую роль в стратегии восстановления европейских государств. Каковы мнения региональных административных элит по экономическому регулированию, роли правительства и свободного рынка? Являются ли эти взгляды связанными с (1) ранней социализацией, (2) образованием, (3) профессиональными интересами, или (4) способностями их администраций? Чтобы ответить на эти вопросы, мы собрали уникальные данные путем опроса 742 административных элит из 63 регионов и 11 стран. Мы находим некоторые подтверждающие доказательства для всех четырех объяснений. Тем не менее, в то время как индивидуальные характеристики этих элит важны, контекстуальные факторы имеют большее значение.

t: The Bite of Administrative Burden: A Theoretical and Empirical Investigation
abs: The study of administrative burden—experienced in individual encounters with government—is being renewed with new theoretical developments and policy applications. Building on recent developments, this article aims to broaden the conceptual framing of administrative burden and extend its empirical investigation beyond concerns about access to and efficiency of public services to questions of individual and societal impacts. It also expands beyond the typical US or developed country context to examine this phenomenon in the setting of a large social protection program in South Africa, where the “bite” of administrative burden may potentially be bigger. The empirical analysis uses data from the South African Child Support Grant (CSG) evaluation to investigate how CSG program rules and requirements affected administrative burdens and erected barriers to grant receipt. The findings show that 60% of CSG recipients experienced an interruption or disconnection in grant receipt that appears to be associated with administrative burden, with 80% of those stoppages in error. The resulting loss of monthly benefits has significant negative implications for the outcomes of adolescents targeted by the program.

t: Managing the Supreme Court: The Chief Justice, Management, and Consensus
abs: In this article, we draw on a prominent model of public management to develop a preliminary theoretical approach to understanding the role of the chief justice in Supreme Court decision-making. In particular, we argue that the Court may seek legitimacy through greater unanimity and discuss how the leadership of the chief justice can facilitate that effort. We assess a hypothesis derived from this theory, showing greater agreement among the justices as the incumbent chief justice’s tenure in office increases. We argue that these results provide support for further attention to and development of a public administration-based approach to the study of Supreme Court decision-making. The application of public administration to judicial politics provides further evidence of management dynamics in American institutions.

t: Mary Parker Follett on the Need to Associate with Gusto
abs: In the study of public administration much attention has been given to networks, collaborative governance (and governance in general) and management, citizen participation, and workplace democracy. The work of Mary Parker Follett has attracted much attention since the 1980s, first in business schools, and then in public administration programs. Her ideas about participative democracy, circular response, and integration as dynamics upon which policy can and ought to be made, about the importance of developing policy on the basis of desires and needs of target groups, and about letting the existing situation determine what action(s) to take (i.e., the law of the situation) have become in our day and age more important and realistic than in her own time. She is very much in sync with ideas percolating in the rapidly industrializing and urbanizing society in which she grew up, and they coalesce around the concept of association. She was not the first to recognize the importance of groups or associations. Following his travels in the United States, Alexis de Tocqueville wrote Democracy in America, a very perceptive study of the American polity as seen through the eyes of a 28-year old Frenchman from a country still reeling from the shockwaves of the French Revolution. Ideals and ideas most associated with that event are liberty, equality, and fraternity. He urges that for democracy to work, people must learn to associate and learn from each other (Tocqueville 2000, 490). In a democracy “…associations must take the place of the powerful particular persons whom equality of conditions has made disappear.” and thus in democracies “…the science of association is the mother science […] the art of associating must be developed and perfected among them…” (ibid., 492; emphasis added). It is at the time of the American and French Revolutions (or, following the American historian Joel Palmer, the “Atlantic Revolutions”) that for the first time the idea emerges that political institutional arrangements can be made on the basis of liberty, equality, and fraternity. How to actually do so, and what it takes, has been the object of attention in political theory and administrative practice ever since. De Tocqueville stopped at concluding that a science of association was necessary for democracy to succeed; several authors since have embraced that thought and provided building blocks for it. One of those is Mary Parker Follett whose books (with the exception of her study of the Speakership), articles, and lectures have been digested and re-created in the study by Stout and Love. This is book is a welcome addition to the Follett literature, in that it provides a book-length study of her ideas and is written by two public administration scholars. Where Joan Tonn’s 2003 intellectual biography of Follett focuses on her organizational and management ideas, Stout and Love present the foundations (i.e., ontology, psychosocial elements, views on science) upon which those ideas rest. They also use their extensive exegesis to provide a “correct” representation of Follett’s views since they find that authors frequently summarize her ideas accurately, but interpret them incorrectly (p. 4). In an endorsement at the back-cover of this book I write that Follett provides the building blocks for a science of association and that the Stout/Love volume “…provides a wonderful entry into the holistic depth and breadth of Follett’s thought…” I wrote that as someone interested in this type of study; the more “distant” role of book reviewer requires an assessment of the Stout/Love study in its contribution to the study of public administration. Stout and Love carefully construct Follett’s worldview as one that is grounded in clear ontological principles of holism (dualisms and hierarchy are impossible), dynamic becoming (think of Heraclitus), and circular response (people act and react in relation to one another and in relation to the situation) (pp. 24–9). These ontological principles translate into features of psychosocial theory, the core of which is that people create each other through circular response and operate in thoughtful groups rather than in crowds, herds, masses, and mobs (pp. 39–51). The traditional “power-over” perspective upon human relations, expressing a hierarchical and individualistic approach to authority, should be replaced by “power-with” which emphasizes that productive relations can (and ought to) be non-hierarchical and propelled by the “law of the situation” (p. 33). This ontology and co-creation activity translates into an epistemology that is based in the notion that knowledge is constantly being created and re-created through active experimentation and integration (p. 66).(On a side note, it is stunning to see how a quantum perspective upon social science where individuals are in a constant state of Becoming is reminiscent of Follett; see Wendt, 2015, p. 207.) Indeed, Mary Parker Follett is highly critical of the one-sided appreciation for rationalism, empiricism, and idealism since the 17th century (p. 67), and seeks to offer for social life an alternative of “genuine democracy” where all stakeholders (people, experts, public officeholders) are involved in creating their social environment (p. 82, 126), where the elites are part of a new process of democracy (p. 117), where law is an evolving and relational practice (p. 94; she is an admirer of Roscoe Pound), where people interact on the basis of sincerity and honesty (p. 103), where cut-throat competition is replaced by cooperative competition (p. 150), where leadership is facilitative (also think of: servant and shared leadership) rather than top-down (p. 172), and where government functions like a community (p. 180: what Follett calls Service State). The preceding paragraph provides a very brief, and probably unsatisfactory, summary of Follett’s rich thoughts, and the reader will get a more complete sense when picking up the Stout/Love study and, of course, by reading Follett first-hand. I liked the Stout-love book because it feeds into my interests in the nature of the study of public administration, the intellectual development of the study and of the role and position of government in society. As with any study, though, there are some concerns. One issue is that the audience targeted by this book is unclear. If it is for scholars in public and business administration, one would expect much more attention to Follett’s influence upon organization and management thought. The reader must wait, however, until chapter 9 before that is addressed, because Stout and Love felt it necessary to spend ample time on her philosophy. This is fine, but the authors do not really target an audience of philosophers either. Follett’s familiarity with philosophical literature is clear, for instance, in her comment as that the relation between conception (hypothesis) and perception (testing) is problematic in the scientific method because of its linearity, and that both are always engaged in circular response (p. 70). The philosopher would like to have seen that this echoes Immanuel Kant’s observation as that perception without conception is blind, and that conception without perception is empty (as mentioned in: Dewey 1910, 272). If anything, Mary Parker Follett is a social commentator and a child of her time whose thoughts about community and society resonated with contemporary reader and authorship. Her thoughts are as relevant in today’s society with its increased emphasis on citizen participation. But, this book is not written for an audience of citizens either, since they would benefit from more attention to how Follett’s thought can be actualized. Her ideas about how a democratic society ought to function are very American: a strong emphasis on self-government (cf. Jefferson), joint ownership of the production process, and joint ownership of democracy. In that spirit Follett insisted that workers and managers should jointly control the workplace (i.e., factory) (p. 151), something that was attempted in former Yugoslavia; and in that spirit she advocated that all people, whichever their role (citizen, official, expert), should engage in the production of democracy. When Follett expresses the need that elites should embrace the new democracy, she reminds of De Tocqueville who also had suggested that the powerful particular persons should be replaced by associations. Her emphasis on community, collaboration, and continuous evolution in and of social relations, is based on widespread concern that authors as scholars or as social commentators on both sides of the Atlantic had about the extent to which industrialization had alienated people from one another and from the work process and, more in general, about the shift from an organic community of people to a mechanistic society of autonomous individuals. Follett’s thoughts about society are reminiscent of Ferdinand Tönnies’ analysis of the change from Gemeinschaft to Gesellschaft and of Émile Durkheim’s notion that we have moved from living in an organic society to one that is mechanistic. They and Follett want to recapture that community element in societal life. Her views of science are very similar to those of Max Weber: developing a social science in its own right, not as a copy of the natural sciences. While critical of aspects of pragmatism (p. 67) she is also influenced by it. For instance, her “law of the situation” harkens back to John Dewey’s “…the criterion of the truth or falsity of meaning, of the adequacy, of the cognitional thing lies within the relationships of the situation and not without” (Dewey 1910, 107; emphasis added). This notion of the “law of the situation” was of rather recent origin, and—as Dewey showed (1910)—inspired by Charles Darwin’s theories that included the idea that organisms adapt to their environment and that they shape their environment in turn. Although Stout and Love present Follett as an original thinker, perhaps even philosopher, it seems that she is much more a social commentator and visionary who builds upon her own experiential knowledge, then contemplates upon what she sees around her, then tries to make sense of it by drawing upon a variety of knowledge sources and elements, and finally integrates these into a worldview for and of a new democracy. According to Stout and Love, Follett drew upon a various knowledge sources and elements: ontology, epistemology, ethics, political and economic theory, biology, psychology, sociology, philosophy, theology, quantum physics, and Eastern, feminist and indigenous spirituality (p. 225). This is a lot, and it is quite eclectic. It would have helped the reader who is not particularly familiar with Follett and/or ideas and concerns in her time about the direction society was taking, to see a more systematic presentation of her ideas by showing what sources she explicitly drew from (e.g., Kant, Dewey, Pound) and implicitly embraced (e.g., De Tocqueville, Tönnies, Durkheim, Weber) and then show how she shaped these “inputs” into a worldview of her own. It is not important to determine how original she was; indeed, Fry and Raadschelders (2014) show that scholars important to the history of the study of public administration (including Follett) drew upon existing ideas and their own experiences that they then cobbled together in a coherent and systematic research agenda. Another concern is that Stout and Love claim that Follett’s interpretive method is quite reminiscent of Max Weber’s idealtyping (p. 13). To be sure, an idealtype is a sublimation of reality, a condensed and idealized version of elements characteristic of a social phenomenon. Weber elaborated Georg Jellinek’s ideas about idealtype as a method, and hoped that it would do for the social sciences what symbols and mathematical formulae had done for the physical sciences. What Follett offers is a utopia, an ideal society where people treat each other out of a fundamental respect for each other’s humanity. That is not an idealtype, it is an ideal. And, it is important to read Follett for that reason. Her utopia is a soothing balm in an age where the traditional agricultural economy with its physical community is replaced by industrial production and anonymity of relations in the urban environment. How realistic her vision is cannot be determined, for societal life today is as much “governed” by hierarchy and social stratification as ever. A final concern is the tone of the volume. Stout and Love clearly set out on a quest to set the record straight on Follett’s behalf, and their writing style is very strident and insistent. That they admire Follett is fine, but that comes at the expense of providing a balanced account of her work by blending appreciation with critique. Instead, and as I mentioned above, they critique others for not interpreting Follett correctly. I could not help checking the critique they had upon the Fry/Raadschelders discussion of Follett’s work (various places on pp. 214–42). Indeed, in one instance Fry and I were inconsistent (“intersubjective assessment of the situation” v. “objective demands of the work situation,” as they report on p. 214), but in the other instances the parts they quoted from our Follett chapter in Mastering Public Administration are quoted out of context. They note that our reasoning displays a “static ontology, atomistic individualism, and positivist epistemology […] but without self-reflection” (p. 222). What fun to find that I must be difficult to pigeon-hole. Am I a positivist as they suggest, or a postmodernist as Riccucci (2010, 118) believes? Another example of such cherry-picking is the following: Roll and Thomas (2014) [suggest] that Follett’s vision of the New State “is today more realistic than at the time of its conception” (p. 254). What Roll and Thomas actually wrote is: “‘The New State’ may never be a reality, but it is today more realistic than at the time of its conception” (Roll and Thomas 2014, 180). And, I cannot help wondering what Stout and Love would think of Evans’ (1998) PhD dissertation in which she analyzed what Dewey and Follett had to offer a new democracy. I was surprised that it was not included in their study, especially since Evans so succinctly captures Follett’s thinking (1998, esp. chap. 7). So what is my recommendation and expectation? I liked reading this book, and that is because I am interested in the intellectual history of public administration as a study and in the development of government’s role and position over time. Colleagues who share these interests will enjoy Stout and Love. However, and in the more evaluative role of a book reviewer, I expect that this book will not conquer a large public administration audience, simply because it is written in the style of a believer rather than in the more distant, weighing type of argument one can expect from the traditional (?) scholar. Will it reach an audience outside of academe? I doubt that, and that is because—paradoxically—the book is too academic in content and style. However, as much as I am a citizen (although of another country), I may not be the right person to assess whether citizens would benefit.

t: The Intellectual Structure of Empirical Network Research in Public Administration
abs: The rapid growth of network research in public administration calls for a systematic review of existing network scholarship. We performed bibliometric analysis and content analysis to identify the research that has had impact on empirical network research in public administration. We examined the key theoretical foundations of existing network research with a focus on empirical network articles that used social network analysis in their methods. We examined the evolution of network scholarship in public administration, identified key network concepts, and analyzed the research clusters. We further identified research gaps in existing empirical network literature and proposed some ideas or topics for future research.

t: The Emergence of Collaborations
abs: In the literature on collaborative governance, it is often assumed that collaborative capacity (i.e., the ability of actors to coordinate their activities around public issues in a collaborative fashion) is primarily generated during the collaborative process itself. In this article, we show that collaborative capacity can already emerge before the start of collaborations, in the form of a common ground and the bridging position that some actors attain through their involvement in different projects that build up to the collaboration. We introduce a conceptual framework that captures these dimensions of collaborative capacity, and we present findings on two case studies to test several propositions, using an approach called event sequence analysis. We find that in both cases a common ground develops before the start of collaborations and influences the aims that are chosen during the collaborations themselves. We also find that actors that attain a bridging position before the collaboration play an important role in assembling building blocks for collaboration together. Our findings have relevance primarily for regional collaborations that involve large numbers of professional organizations. В литературе по совместному управлению, часто предполагается, что потенциал к сотрудничеству (т.е. способность субъектов координировать свою деятельность вокруг общественных вопросов в формате совместного сотрудничества), в первую очередь генерируется в ходе самого процесса сотрудничества. В этой статье мы покажем, что совместный потенциал уже может появиться до начала сотруднических отношений, в виде общей основы и обоюдных позиций, которые могут сформироваться между некоторыми участниками в ходе работы в различных проектах до установления сотруднических отношений. Мы выдвигаем концептуальный остов, который захватывает эти аспекты потенциала для совместного сотрудничества, и представляем результаты на примере двух исследований где мы тестируем несколько предположений, используя подход, называемый анализ последовательности событий. Мы находим, что в обоих примерах общая основа развивается до начала сотрудничества и влияет на цели, которые выбираются в ходе самого сотрудничества. Мы также находим, что участники, которые находятся в позиции связующего звена до сотруднических отношений играют важную роль при подборке «строительных блоков» для совместной работы. Наши выводы в первую очередь имеют актуальность для межрегиональных сотруднических отношений, включающих большое количество профессиональных организаций.

t: Breaking the Silence: How Conversations about Race Can Influence Work Practices and Interactions
abs: I recently attended a workshop that addressed how faculty can effectively lead class discussions about workplace diversity. One objective was creating a “safe environment” in the classroom so that students can engage in authentic dialogue. A striking question asked by several audience members was “how do we initiate the conversation about race?” There we were, many of us experienced instructors and researchers of workplace diversity, yet still uncertain about how or where to start. Imagine how much more difficult such conversations are in various workplaces where talking about race is often taboo, even in those that espouse a commitment to diversity, and where employees are not “experts” in diversity. How often do employees believe that discussions about race and ethnicity are important, but remain silent for lack of knowing how to begin, let alone knowing whether it is “safe” or “appropriate” to do so? How many wish they could ask questions so that they better understand a perspective or experience, but are afraid of unintentionally offending a colleague? And what opportunities are missed as a result? Finally, how much longer can we sidestep these discussions? Authors Erica Gabrielle Foldy and Tamara R. Buckley explain that such employees as caught in a color bind, reluctant to discuss or simply not discussing race or culture even when they think it is important. Their book, The Color Bind: Talking (and Not Talking) About Race at Work, offers a much needed contribution to our understanding of racial and culturally based workplace exchanges and practices. Foldy and Buckley build theory based on a longitudinal, comparative case study of seven teams of social workers in a child welfare agency. Foldy’s access to the organization offered a unique opportunity for an ethnographic study of racial and cultural practices in public sector work. As such, Foldy and Buckley’s findings possess a depth that, to the best of my knowledge, other recent studies about race and culture in public organizations cannot match. Their arguments are grounded in the core concepts of color blindness and color cognizance, drawing from fields such as sociology, political science, management, social work, and psychology. Foldy and Buckley define color blindness as the belief that race and ethnicity are largely irrelevant and that racism and discrimination are facets of the past (p. 14). They explain color cognizance as the belief that racial and cultural differences are important because of their impact on individuals, groups, and communities (p. 14). This study does not assess whether the teams are culturally competent, which the authors explain is about recognizing the importance of race and ethnicity with full knowledge or skill (p. 23). Instead the authors focus on how color blindness and color cognizance play out in day-to-day work interactions, building theory about “what enables and inhibits color-cognizant practice in work groups” (p. 32). Three chapters focus on findings from three of the four teams for which the authors performed an in-depth study. Each team presents a different level of racial-cultural practice based on the authors’ analysis: color cognizant, color hostile, and color evasive. From their findings, Foldy and Buckley identify two team characteristics that, along with the team leadership and the organizational environment, are critical for moving beyond the color bind. One factor is a climate of safety, or the extent to which employees may voice what they think and be authentic selves without penalty or sanction. The second factor is a learning environment, which the authors state is not possible without a sense of safety. They also note that teams must also have at least some members who are color cognizant in order to transcend the color bind. I was particularly struck by their finding of color minimization, where the importance of race and culture are initially acknowledged and then downplayed. Their findings and analysis culminate in a multilevel model of team racial-cultural practice. A core strength of The Color Bind is the longitudinal design and ethnographic methods employed by Foldy and Buckley. Foldy collected data over 4 years through observation of organizational and team meetings, individual and team interviews, and the collection of organizational documents. Doing so enabled the authors to examine sensemaking and the enactment of race and culture from multiple lenses and at the individual and team levels within the broader organizational and office contexts. A great deal of the book’s power lies in the data itself. Each chapter opens with the unfolding of team dialogue in action or quotes from the interviews. These accounts are powerful, and sometimes surprising, discussions of race and culture. Foldy and Buckley illustrate ways that race and culture were directly considered and discussed by the social workers and managers as well as “avoidance techniques” used by the employees. The data place the reader firmly in the situation and aptly support Foldy and Buckley’s main points. The data and analysis offer an in-depth view of how race and culture are discussed in everyday team interactions and practices. Many studies about team and organizational diversity use quantitative data to test hypotheses about outcomes such as pay disparity, career advancement, or team effectiveness. But such studies fall short of revealing the processes at the root of “what is going on” (Corbin and Strauss 2008, 72) within the organization. Foldy and Buckley offer thick, rich description of the interpersonal interactions that shape daily worklife that cannot be drawn from quantitative data. Their approach is particularly unique within the public management literature where many studies have drawn upon representative bureaucracy theory and quantitative data to focus on how the presence of racial or ethnic minorities shapes outcomes (Bradbury and Kellough 2011; Watkin-Hayes 2011). However, these studies neglect to examine the underlying processes that can influence practice and outcomes (Watkins-Hayes 2011). Thus although this literature can provide insight into the positive effects of representative bureaucracy, it does not adequately explain the underlying interactional dynamics (Kennedy 2013; Watkins-Hayes 2011). Although Foldy and Buckley’s work does not focus on outcomes, it contributes toward filling this gap so that we can begin to better link practices to results. I especially appreciated the authors’ openness about their differences as an interracial research team and how they learned from each other. Foldy and Buckley themselves break the color bind as they frankly discuss their “tussles” (their word) as they wrote this book. As such, they themselves embody the complexities and contradictions of a color-cognizant approach. And in doing so, they, perhaps inadvertently, hold themselves out as the very role models they call for to break the color bind at work—those individuals who “model that these issues matter and are discussable” (p. 161). Foldy and Buckley nicely anticipate questions that readers may ask. As I was reading this book I found myself taking a critical eye and asking “What about the intersectionality of race and gender (or class, religion, sexual orientation)?” “What about the effects of leadership?” “What about the nature of the organizational context (one in which race is or can be salient due to the very nature of the work)?” and “How do the organizational subcultures of the different offices influence the conversations about race?” Nearly every question I raised was addressed by the authors in some form. However, although Foldy and Buckley discuss the deliberate decision not to focus on intersectionality, I wish it had been given more attention. They offer compelling arguments as to why a focus on race and culture is particularly important. But many scholars, including Foldy and Buckley, recognize that race and ethnicity are not isolated constructs (Bearfield 2009; Collins 1986, 1993; Crenshaw 1990; Stivers 2002) and as such I argue that the examination of race as a stand-alone factor may not fully capture the phenomenon in question. And, in fact, Foldy and Buckley do bring in other dimensions of diversity when relevant to their analysis. Future studies could and should extend Foldy and Buckley’s theory by considering intersectionality. Although their goal is clearly theory-building, Foldy and Buckley do not neglect the importance of implications for practice. They translate their multilevel model into suggestions for practice at the individual, group, and organizational levels. They call for both formal and informal leaders to take an active role in developing color-cognizant practices. Foldy and Buckley also take on the ubiquitous diversity training offered by organizations by suggesting that such sessions focus more on exploring practices rather than “exhorting employees to think and act differently” (p. 162). I have two minor critiques to share. First, I wish the authors provided a more explanation as to why Team Southwest (one of the four in-depth teams) is relegated to an online appendix. Appendix B offers a somewhat vague explanation referring to clarity and parsimony and that Team Southwest’s practice was color evasive similar to one of the other teams. I read the online appendix and I recognize that this decision may have been driven by many factors. But I would have preferred more explanation in the main narrative as to why it was not included. Second, as I read the book, I kept referring back to the early chapters for definitions of terms as a ‘refresher.’ Several times I wished I had a “glossary of terms” to which I could quickly refer to quickly compare and contrast definitions or refresh my memory. This issue is minor, however, and certainly is not one that detracts from the book’s overall contribution or message. Foldy and Buckley clearly state that their purpose is not to link color cognizance to outcomes, and in their concluding chapter they propose future studies investigate links between racial-cultural practices and outcomes. But I would argue that we first need greater understanding of how difference is brought to bear in work practices across different organizational contexts. As Watkins-Hayes (2011, i235) notes, understanding how race is employed in the encounters between clients and caseworkers and between caseworkers themselves can reveal the importance of race for client outcomes. Foldy and Buckley move us a long way toward this understanding, but there is still more we can learn. Additional in-depth studies about how difference is enacted and shapes workplace interactions and inclusion in public sector organizations is sorely needed. One could argue that by definition the context of a child welfare agency and teams of social workers is one in which race and culture are likely to be discussed. As Foldy and Buckley note in their concluding chapter, they present a conceptual framework through which we can study other organizational contexts, determining how and whether the theory applies and then extending it. Overall, I highly recommend this book both for researchers and as course reading. The public management and public administration diversity literature would do well to “take a page” from Foldy and Buckley’s book. A recent review noted that past work published in public management journals on race and ethnicity has focused predominantly on workforce trends, affirmative action, and active representation (Pitts and Wise 2010). Public sector workplaces tend to be more diverse than the private sector (Riccucci 2009), but most public sector studies do not explain how difference is experienced within public organizations or how it influences work practices and everyday interactions. In-depth studies like Foldy and Buckley’s portray employee sensemaking about difference at work and how difference is enacted in interpersonal interactions and work practices. This grounding is needed to enable change toward more inclusive workplace environments and so that organizations can best serve a diverse array of constituents. But such research is hard—both in the research process itself and in the dissemination of findings. Readers will find that Foldy and Buckley offer a rich, informed basis that should invigorate and unbind us to pursue such studies head on.

t: Of Fergusons: Blunting Racialized Predatory Policing
abs: Urban teens and young adults are particularly susceptible to the judgments and decisions of the state’s frontline workforce. We know this in the extreme as I began contemplating this review with events unfolding nationally in and around the fatal shooting of Michael Brown and a grand jury’s declination to indict Ferguson, Missouri Officer Daren Wilson. A few of these events occurred eyes wide open. At the time, my home office looked out over Telegraph Avenue, just a stone’s throw north of the Oakland Border where, literally, twice the Berkeley Police Department confronted scores of young people attempting to breech the ramp to Route 24, a main artery to the Bay Bridge, and disrupt holiday traffic as an assertive protest tactic. Rather than an old lefty on the streets with the protesters, I joined a group of locals who hang out at the storefront indie coffeehouse of my multiuse, loft building, spelling the owners who needed rest after a couple nights of protecting their businesses against fringe vandalism that always accompanies committed protest activities. I, like many of the older Telegraph crowd, became bystanders to the youth-led rebellion sparked by Ferguson. Most of the time, I stayed holed up in my home office, pondering work and longing for holiday in the desert while gazing out my loft window. Initial inspiration for this project came to me in one of these moments as my eyes moved iteratively from the protesters to the frontline workforce assigned to control them. A number of my Cal-Berkeley students come from ethno-racially mixed urban families and are active protesters passionately committed to reversing the long-standing assault on African American and Latino/a youth by our state institutions. At the same time, my ties run deep to frontline workers who are the faces and agents of these state institutions, law enforcement to public education. When street confrontations occur, the social distance between workers and protesters appears as a chasm. But, in fact, the gap between the protesters and the workers I know is also razor thin; a good number of my urban students enter the state, frontline workforce as teachers, cops, social workers, probation officers, public defenders, and youth counselors for nonprofits. Like Victor Rios, a Latino urban ethnographer, many of them credit the mentorship of frontline workers, including cops, for their making it to university while pointing to contrary experiences that pulled them and many of their friends in the direction of experiencing the state as a “youth control complex,” the sum of encounters with the frontline workforce that “… collectively punish, stigmatize, monitor, and criminalize young people in an attempt to control them” (Rios 2011, 40). The contradictory ways street-level workers influence the life trajectories of young people coupled with the strong draw of conscientious urban college graduates to this line of work form contours of my own inquiry over the last decade. Zachary Oberfield’s project was already on my radar as relevant to these issues, leading me to order a copy of Becoming Bureaucrats ahead of an email from Mary Feeney asking me to review his book. It was easy to say yes at that moment and now, a few months later (thanks Mary), I report on Zach’s framing of worker socialization, his logic of inquiry and what he discovers about “… who bureaucrats are and how they are ‘made,’” (Oberfield 2014, 2), the principal purpose of his monograph. I will tell you now that it is a richly researched study of socialization well worth reading. After explaining why this book deserves your attention and offering some critique (the essential requirements of a book reviewer), I draw broadly on my knowledge of frontline inquiry and policing to gain purchase on “Fergusons” or what I regard as organizational pathologies that constitute young people as materialized objects of racialized predatory policing practices and set in motion their mobilization to challenge these conditions in the streets. My emphasis is on both understanding and blunting these organizational pathologies. I apologize in advance for dragging Zack Oberfield, in the form of his book, into this topic, but clear connections are made to his work. Drawing on an extensive literature cutting across a number of fields and disciplines, Oberfield puts forward two ways to think about the making of frontline workers—they bring a dispositional perspective to the job that is a reflection of the web of their social histories in contrast to an institutional perspective that imagines work orientations shaped by bureaucratic structures, norms, and processes (2014, 2–4; 22–38). To determine which or what blend of socialization forces matter, he investigates “motivations” or why people enter frontline work, their “attitudes” toward the citizenry they serve, and their “identities” or sense of self-understanding about doing this kind of work (2014, 10) over time. That’s right, he tracks the continuity and change in motivations, attitudes, and identities of cohorts of law enforcement personnel and social caseworkers from entry through 2 years on the job. Implementation of this creative design enables Zach to make well-grounded claims about how much workers’ everyday judgments and practices are shaped by social biographies and organizational manipulations. And, like a triathlete, he complements his survey skills with worker interviews and finishes off his investigative run in “observant participation” (2014, 192) undergoing training and working in a social welfare office for a year.1 I challenge colleagues to find a more robust commitment to going the distance in service to the study of frontline work. Oberfield stays true to tracking workers’ self-described motivations, attitudes, and identities over time, but oddly decides to bring these elements together under the umbrella of “bureaucratic personality” rather than defending them as traits of long-term socialization. In 1940, Robert K. Merton signaled a worry about state agencies becoming overly focused on rule following and routinized processing of cases over the human qualities of client expectations and needs. He introduced the notion of a “bureaucratic personality” to signal his concern that bureaucracies may select a kind of person who is easily indoctrinated to give “… primary concern with conformity to the rules [such that it] interferes with the achievement of the purposes of the organization” (Merton 1940, 563). Merton’s questions at the end of his essay call for an investigation of how state organizations select and indoctrinate who they hire when he asks—“To what extent are particular personality types selected and modified by the various bureaucracies … and in as much as ascendancy and submission are held to be traits of personality, … do bureaucracies select personalities of particularly submissive or ascendant tendencies?” (1940, 568). Oberfield is rightly interested in rule following, but his work is not an investigation of bureaucratic selection or a search for a kind of psychological make-up among frontline workers who, in Merton’s words, are “particularly submissive” to bureaucratic norms. Instead of concentrating on organizational selection processes, including the deployment of psychological testing tools, Oberfield’s empirical work is on the self-reported attitudes of workers about what they bring to the job as social beings and how steady they hold to these attitudes over 2 years in the job. Late in the monograph, he explicitly acknowledges that his survey focuses on socialization and that given his tools of inquiry, “… it is not possible to say whether or how personality played a role in entrant development” (Oberfield, 2014, 170).2 We all know that the concepts (and research questions) we deploy in our publications have been backward mapped onto the discoveries we achieve through the analysis of our empirical data. Oberfield’s time series of who workers are and how they are made points strongly away from the idea of indoctrinated bureaucrats and instead, firmly establishes state frontline workers defined by the kind of citizens they are upon entering public service. So, on empirical grounds as well, why introduce the idea of the bureaucratic personality? More on this obsession of mine below, but first, let’s turn to his insightful findings. Oberfield finds more continuity than change, that is, workers’ motivations, attitudes, and identities hold quite steady over the course of their training and through 2 years on the job. Focusing on police officers and social workers, he finds that most entrants “… are strongly influenced by where they started” (2014, 169) holding to the motivations, attitudes, and identities that they express at entry over the course of 2 years. He uses “differential continuity” to note that both the groups of cops and caseworkers he surveys show modest shifts in motivation and attitudes “fairly early” (in training or soon after) while individuals remain in a similar position over time relative to their self-revelations at entering public service (2014, 169). Both cops and welfare caseworkers do not develop the identities of bureaucratic rule followers and instead, their dependency on rules “wanes with time” as they draw more upon their personal identities to “… read the people and situations they encounter on a daily basis” (Oberfield 2014, 139). As for worker attitudes, the demeanor displayed by citizens they encounter shapes judgments more than assessments of the structural conditions, the social and economic inequalities related that give shape to everyday conditions of life. The workers in his study bring to the job the dominant American view that social problems are more a result of individual choices and this perspective is echoed in interactions with trainers, supervisors, and peers on the job (Oberfied 2014, 162–3). With these overall findings, why not refrain from referencing these public employees as “bureaucrats” realizing that how a target group is socially constructed has serious implications for both the benefits and burdens they will acquire (Schneider and Ingram 1997, 102–49)? Certainly, academic use of “bureaucrats” to depict public employees who interact directly with the citizenry evolves from Lipsky’s classic study of Street-Level Bureaucracy (1980, 2010) and perhaps Max Weber’s own depictions of bureaucracies (Weber 1946a, 1946b, translated by Gerth and Mills, 221–44). But, this linguistic characterization also contributes to “bureaucracy bashing” by media pundits and politicians (Hubbell 1991) with the goal of undermining social services, often with effect. For that reason, my principal colleague related to this line of inquiry, Steven Maynard-Moody, and I have shifted to use “frontline work and workers” and “citizen agents” with serious purpose and empirical grounding as described below (Maynard-Moody and Musheno 2003, 2012; Musheno and Maynard-Moody 2015). Caseworkers. Consider as well Oberfield’s depiction of welfare caseworkers based on his time-series survey. They are drawn to this profession mostly by “egoistic motives,” specifically job benefits, while giving greater weight to helping clients and treating people fairly as they take on the job. Emphasis on helping clients and fair treatment diminishes after 2 years and instead getting owed benefits to clients while monitoring them for fraud ascends in importance. Oberfield associates the strong draw to job benefits, a motivation that remains dominant throughout the study period, with the fact that many workers come from poor family backgrounds and have histories of receiving welfare in their personal biographies. That is, their social histories define their draw and orientation toward the job. But, even with these personal histories, caseworkers see welfare claiming as a product of individual, bad decision-making (Oberfield 2014, 162). Ironically, they, like most Americans, hold to the view that humans are autonomous beings making their own destinies. Though only faintly evident in Oberfield’s study, other scholars studying social workers have tracked how the institutional shift from welfare to workfare has altered the job from field centered around client needs to office centered around surveillance of clients for conformity to job-related requirements and fraud detection (Soss, Fording, and Schram 2011). At the same time, scholars studying the shift to workfare uncover substantial numbers of workers who undermine computerized accountability to meet their judgments about client needs. t: Should We Build It? Will They Come?
abs: In Field of Dreams, the sound of James Earl Jones’s supernatural basso profundo declaration to Kevin Costner’s Ray Kinsella, “People will come, Ray” is etched in our cultural consciousness. Less well-remembered is Timothy Busfield’s warning, “You’ll lose everything Ray.” Arts and culture leaders considering a capital building project would do better to have Peter Frumkin and Ana Kolendo on their shoulders whispering, “Seek strategic alignment,” rather than believing in either binary outcome of a fantasy. Successful cultural infrastructure projects are not fields of dreams but rather, as Frumkin and Kolendo assert, the result of the strategic alignment of mission, capacity, community, and funding. The Cultural Policy Center at University of Chicago launched a study in 2007 of cultural building projects. The research found that there was a building boom during the period under study, 1994–2008, and especially 1998–2001, but that the increase in cultural infrastructure did not have discernible spillover effects in surrounding communities nor was there significant changes in the number of arts organizations as a result ( Woronkowicz et al. 2012 ). When the Center’s report Set in Stone: Building America’s New Generation of Arts Facilities 1998–2008 was released, it hit the nonprofit arts funding community like a load of bricks. I immediately added its case studies, which are authored by Frumkin and Kolendo, to my arts management syllabus. Janet Brown, President and CEO of Grantmakers in the Arts wrote at the time of the report’s release, “I cannot stress enough how important this study is for our field right now… It points out how vulnerable organizations are when moving into a major capital commitment and stresses the need for realistic financial planning beyond the scope of the building project” ( Brown 2012 ). Many in the arts community knew anecdotally or intuitively that a new building will not solve an organization’s problems and could instead cause years of operational deficits, community acrimony, mission drift, or even dissolution. The Set in Stone report confirmed this intuition. It also promised further research, including two books, “one about the strategic management of these projects, and the other about the broader impacts these projects have on the nation’s cultural ecology” (p. 34). Frumkin and Kolendo’s Building for the Arts: The Strategic Design of Cultural Facilities is the first of these. Understandably, Frumkin and Kolendo advocate for a strategic, rather than “field of dreams,” approach to capital building projects. They define strategic design as “the moment when an arts organization brings into alignment, fit, and coherence its mission, capacity, funding, and community to realize a capital project” (p. 10). Design, however, is a process , not a moment. Despite this semantic misstep, the authors describe that process in the more than a dozen case studies they draw upon to illustrate their proposition. More than once, we are reminded that the alignment that supports capital building success is “a continuum, not a binary” (p. 225). With one exception, the case studies included in the book do not replicate the material already published in the Set in Stone report, even when focused on institutions previously studied. Frumkin and Kolendo use the case studies to illustrate the constituent parts of the build-or-don’t-build decision (Chapter 2) and each of the four elements of strategic design (fundraising, capacity, community, and mission, each elucidated in Chapters 3 through 6). They smartly use at least two different building types in each chapter, usually a museum or collection venue and a performing arts center or theater. One of the more interesting pairings is in the penultimate chapter 7, which focuses on the overall process of seeking strategic alignment. Here the authors delve deep into two organizations in Austin, Texas, the Austin Museum of Art and the Long Center for the Performing Arts. By using two case studies with divergent outcomes from the same city, the reader is able to glean a richer context for the case studies, especially with regard to the local fundraising climate and potential for community engagement. My quibble with Building for the Arts is around this issue of community engagement. Chapter 4, “Connecting to Community,” focuses on effectively managing negative reaction to proposed capital projects rather than on positively engaging communities in the strategic design process. To be truly useful to proactive arts leaders, the chapter could have, instead of focusing on managing problems, showcased a case in which the community was engaged for the good. There is such a case in the book, but it is used to illustrate the element of operational capacity, and is positioned as a negative example. However, buried in the story of Lorton Workhouse Art Center, an adaptive reuse of a prison complex, are several examples of proactive community engagement that lead to strategically successful decisions. “She [Irma Clifton] took people on tours of the facilities…She spoke to everyone she could—fellow committee members, each of the county supervisors, Rotary Club, Lion’s Club, business associations…One day, Clifton and McBride walked around the neighborhood and knocked on the door of every home in the Workhouse’s neighborhood…Their goal was to handle any and all opposition pre-emptively. ‘We didn’t want anything popping up at the last minute.’” (p. 153.). With regard to proactively engaging community, as Clifton does, arts and culture leaders—and the public managers who engage with them on cultural building projects—would do well to follow the lead of two seemingly unrelated but compatible practitioners: artists who do community engagement work and entrepreneurship guru, Steve Blank. Artists such as Liz Lerman and Michael Rohd advocate for partnerships between arts organizations and communities that develop by request, by being “invited in” to a community (see, e.g. Rohd 2012 ), while in complementary fashion, Blank, and others who advocate the “lean startup” approach, advise entrepreneurs (and by their own use of the word, Frumkin and Kolendo consider cultural builders to be “entrepreneurs”) to “get out of the building” to test hypotheses about a venture’s value proposition by actually engaging with stakeholders (see, e.g. Blank and Dorf 2012 ). The Workhouse Arts Center case provides an example of both of these approaches, but is not positioned as such. Rather, the management strategy advocated by Frumkin and Kolendo is reactive. They offer sound guidance for prioritizing stakeholder feedback using Mitchell, Agle, and Wood’s (1997) framework categorizing stakeholders as definitive, expectant, or latent with definitive stakeholders having varying degrees of power, legitimacy, and urgency. But, this is guidance to be applied after the fact, when community input is already being received. I wish that Frumkin and Kolendo had offered proactive guidance, readily available from both the arts and entrepreneurship communities of practice. Although the term “arts entrepreneur” is not much used after the first chapter, its use there and, more importantly, the entrepreneurial themes engaged by the book’s case studies, position it as a contribution to the regrettably thin collection of research-based scholarship on arts entrepreneurship. Managing a high level of uncertainty, coping with unpredictable risk, and bundling resources to bring an arts enterprise to fruition are pervading themes throughout Building for the Arts . Frumkin and Kolendo emphasize the importance of the arts entrepreneur (sometimes an individual, but sometimes a small group) in driving a project home, “Absent such initiative and drive, the organizations can struggle and wallow in mediocrity for long periods of time” (p. 16). The well-wrought portraits of some of these actors in the case studies will make several of the cases useful for the growing number of professors teaching arts entrepreneurship coursework. Despite my concern about the framing of community engagement, Building for the Arts makes a significant and much needed contribution to the broader arts management literature, too little of which is based on such in-depth primary research. The case studies can be read both in and out of the academy for lessons not only about capital building and fundraising, but also about managerial decision-making, especially in the nonprofit sector. The richly detailed case studies can be mined further for important lessons on board governance, board relations, and board recruitment. In addition, these case studies offer insight for local policymakers interfacing with arts and culture leaders and the philanthropic community. The strategic alignment of funding, community, organizational capacity, and mission advocated by Frumkin and Kolendo are transferable across the nonprofit and public sectors. The 15 “rules” they promote in conclusion are applicable to any infrastructure project. These rules include “fund operations and endowment as you go” (p. 230), “wait to announce the building budget until you are certain you have a solid number” (p. 235), and “bringing in a star architect will increase building costs (p. 238).” These seem like common sense, but what Frumkin and Kolendo offer is qualitative evidence of their veracity, supported by quantitative evidence in the earlier research. Two of the “rules” specifically refute the epidemic of “If you build it, they will come” thinking that pervaded the arts and culture sector during the building boom: “supply does not create its own demand” (p. 240) and “a great building will not lead to artistic excellence, but a powerful and compelling artistic vision can lead to a new building” (p. 241). Ultimately, this is the alignment that needs to exist: the powerful and compelling artistic vision with…everything else.
