Organizational Capability in the Public Sector: A Configurational Approach
abs: This article brings together resource-based theory and contingency theory to analyze organizational capability in the public sector. Fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis is used to identify configurations of organizational attributes (department size, structural complexity, agencification, personnel instability, use of temporary employees), associated with high and low organizational capability in UK central government departments. Findings identify a single core configuration of organizational attributes associated with high capability departments—low structural complexity and personnel stability. Two core configurations are associated with low capability departments—personnel instability and the combination of structural complexity and departmental agencification. Based on the configurations evident in successful and struggling organizations, discussion illuminates potential organizational design strategies to improve public sector organizational capability.

t: Responsive Change: Agency Output Response to Reputational Threats
abs: How do reputational threats affect agency outputs? We undertake quantitative and qualitative analyses of reputation and outputs data regarding the fight against welfare fraud by the main service delivery agency for the Australian government in the field of social policy. We find that an agency’s response to reputational threats is endogenously differential both within the set of agency outputs and between agency outputs and other activities (a pattern we termed responsive change ). For the former, we find that when an agency output is below average, negative media coverage leads to an increase in output in the following year. However, this relationship is nullified for agency outputs that are about average and is reversed for outputs that are above average, that is, these outputs tend to decrease following negative media coverage. For the latter, we find that when a reputational threat is joined by a general above average level of outputs, the agency’s drive for change is likely to be channeled into activities other than the number of units of service delivered (e.g., public relations, community engagements, stakeholder consultations, etc.).

t: Myths of Accountability and European Agencies
abs: Madalina Busuioc’s 2013 book, European Agencies: Law and Practices of Accountability, is the latest attempt to engage the issue of accountability of European agencies. This book is the result of a long research journey by the author; her academic career began with a PhD dissertation titled “The Accountability of European Agencies: legal provisions and ongoing practices” and since then she has elaborated and fine-tuned her work on the law and, particularly, the practice of accountability relationships of European agencies, becoming an expert in the field. Since the 1990s, the literature on the accountability of European agencies has gained momentum with the boom of “agencification,” the expansion of the competences of the European Union (EU) and the governance turn of EU policy-making (Curtin 2007). Scholars of EU studies have adopted two alternative positions on agency accountability. On the one hand, democratic deficit theorists have supported the view that European agencies lack accountability, due to four reasons: first, their abrupt and ad hoc appearance; second, their non-majoritarian nature, as agencies operate at “arms length” from directly elected principals; third, their ever-growing (quasi-)decision-making powers; and, finally, their lives “in the shadow of the law” (p. 5). Conversely, other scholars rejected both the democratic deficit theory and the idea of agency accountability deficit, asserting that, in order to be efficient, it is fundamental that the EU system is insulated from both political control and stringent accountability mechanisms. According to Busuioc, the assessment of agency accountability requires a common definition of accountability and the examination not only of the existing legal arrangements, but also of the everyday practices of European agencies’ accountability relations, features that have been generally overlooked in the literature.

t: Rethinking New Public Management Delivery Forms and Efficiency: Long-Term Effects in Spanish Local Government: Table 1
abs: With the increase in public services offered at the local level and heightened budgetary and financial constraints on local government, new ways of managing local public services must be sought, in order to maximize the efficiency of resource management. Accordingly, local governments have introduced organizational changes, through contracting out, the creation of public agencies, and increased cooperation with other municipalities and private companies. However, previous studies have only examined the relationship between contracting out and efficiency, and no in-depth survey has been made of the relationship between efficiency with other forms of management, nor of the joint impact of these forms of management on efficiency. The main aim of this study is to determine whether New Public Management (NPM) delivery forms do in fact improve the efficiency of Spanish local governments. In this regard, we analyze the particular impact of the global recession. Our results suggest that in general terms the creation of agencies, contracting out, and intermunicipal cooperation reduce cost efficiency. However, these results also lead to the conclusion that during the global recession, some of these NPM delivery forms tended to become more efficient. Thus, empirical evidence suggests that the adoption of mixed firms contributes to higher levels of cost efficiency in the whole period considered, and thus it may be a suitable instrument in periods of crisis. Com o aumento dos serviços ofertados em nível local, aumentos nos orçamentos e nas restrições orçamentárias nos governos locais, novas formas de gerenciamento de serviços públicos no nível local precisaram ser descobertas a fim de maximizar a eficiência da gestão dos recursos. Dessa forma, governos locais têm introduzido mudanças organizacionais através de terceirizações, criação de agencias públicas e aumento da cooperação com outros municípios e empresas privadas. Contudo, estudos anteriores apenas examinaram o relacionamento entre o processo de contratação e a eficiência, e nenhum levantamento em profundidade foi feito sobre o relacionamento entre eficiência e outras formas de gerenciamento, nem sobre o impacto destas formas de gerenciamento sobre a eficiência. O objetivo principal deste estudo é determinar se formas de prestação de serviços propostas pela Nova Gestão Pública (NPM) realmente melhoram a eficiência de municípios espanhóis. Neste sentido, nós analisamos o impacto particular da recessão global. Nossos resultados sugerem que, em termos gerais, a criação de agencias, terceirização e cooperação intermunicipal reduz a eficiência de custos. Entretanto, estes resultados também levam a concluir que durante a recessão global, algumas destas formas de prestação de serviços via Nova Gestão Pública tendem a se tornar mais eficientes. Assim, as evidências empíricas sugerem que a adoção de organizações mistas contribuem para um nível maior de eficiência de custos em todo o período considerado, e, desta forma, este pode ser um instrumento adequado para períodos de crise. t: The Performance of Performance-Based Contracting in Human Services: A Quasi-Experiment
abs: Performance-based contracting (PBC) is becoming increasingly attractive to public human service agencies. By linking contract compensation to contractors’ performance, PBC is expected to foster quality services, to improve outcomes, and to reduce government monitoring. However, empirical evidence on the effectiveness of PBC remains both limited and mixed. Based on a case study of the Indiana vocational rehabilitation program, this article employs a quasi-experimental design to evaluate the effectiveness of PBC for individual employment outcomes over the 2004–09 period, with the Michigan vocational rehabilitation program as a control. Using propensity score matching and difference-in-differences regressions to control for the imbalances between the two states, this article finds that PBC significantly improves employment results and reduces time to employment, two measured performance indicators. However, the impact of PBC on unmeasured employment quality, as indicated by working hours and wages, is trivial. This article further suggests relational contracting as a supplemental mechanism for PBC in human service provision.

t: Balancing Life on the Tenure Track: Books to Help with Substance and Form
abs: I recall being a PhD student and thinking I could not possibly be any busier. Then I started a tenure-track faculty job at a research university and realized how much “free time” I had as a doctoral student. As a new faculty member, I strive to balance my intellectual development with the reality of juggling research, teaching, and service along with a young family. When I was asked to select and review a book that was “most important/valuable” to me as a new faculty member, I was torn between selecting a book that has facilitated my intellectual growth and one that has helped me balance my various responsibilities. Unable to decide, I chose two books: Wasserman and Faust’s Social Network Analysis: Methods and Applications (1994) and Boice’s Advice for New Faculty Members: Nihil Nimus (2000). The first has been substantively helpful. Wasserman and Faust provide a comprehensive overview of network methods, useful for anyone interested in conducting network analysis in the social sciences. The second has provided valuable insight on how academics can manage research, teaching, and service in their early careers. Advice for New Faculty Members: Nihil Nimus focuses on the process rather than the substance of work, with advice that is relevant across disciplines. Although many books have been valuable to me as an assistant professor, I imagine these books may have wide appeal for JPART readers.

t: Reexamining the Assumptions of Bureaucratic Behavior
“Bureaucracy and Dissent” or “The Ethics of Red Tape”? Linking Red Tape and Guerrilla Government
abs: In considering books I have found valuable in my first few years as a faculty member, two came to mind: Barry Bozeman’s Bureaucracy and Red Tape (2000) and Rosemary O’Leary’s The Ethics of Dissent: Managing Guerrilla Government (2nd ed., 2014). These books were influential early in my graduate career, both informing my dissertation topic and subsequent research agenda. At first blush, it may seem that these books are quite unrelated, but they have more in common than one might expect. Broadly, they both address bureaucracy through their own unique lenses. One addresses a common bureaucratic pathology—red tape—while the other addresses actions within bureaucracy—dissent. These perspectives, along with more traditional bureaucratic theory, are particularly useful as someone who studies organization theory and public ethics. In this review, I first present an overview of each book. Following that, I share some of the common themes I have found particularly compelling and reflect on how and why they have become critical to my work as a junior scholar. I preface this review by cautioning that it is not comprehensive. Because of its reflective nature, I have chosen to focus on the parts of these two books that are salient to my research. Beginning my PhD coursework, I remember being turned off by “red tape.” For my doctoral-level public management course at the University of Kansas, Professor Leisha DeHart-Davis required all of us to review a book and present that review to the class. Unsure of which book to select, Professor DeHart-Davis suggested that I review Bozeman’s (2000) book on red tape given my interest in organization rules. I was hesitant at first because I scoffed at the idea of immersing myself into the theory of “red tape,” the thing everybody seems to hate, but I took her advice. It’s funny to look back and see how my views have changed, considering “red tape” appears nearly 400 times in my dissertation, the title of which includes “red tape.” While Bozeman’s (2000) book is not the first book-length treatment of red tape—Herbert Kaufman’s Red Tape: Its Origins, Uses, and Abuses (1977) came almost 25 years earlier—it is the first to develop a comprehensive theory of red tape. According to Bozeman, Kaufman’s idea that “one man’s red tape is another’s treasured safeguard” (Kaufman 1977, as cited in Bozeman 2000, p. 3) is not reflective of red tape. Instead, red tape is bad, pathological, and there should be “zero tolerance” for it (Bozeman, p. 11). If a rule is viewed as a “treasured safeguard,” Bozeman argues that it is not red tape (p. 3). This distinction is made early on in the first chapter, which is critical for understanding Bozeman’s theory of red tape. After explaining some of the more well-known red tape ideas that had prevailed for decades, Bozeman presents his own “working definition” of red tape: “[r]ules, regulations, and procedures that remain in force and entail a compliance burden but do not advance the legitimate purposes the rules were intended to serve” (p. 12). In setting the stage for a rules-based red tape theory, Bozeman spends some time addressing bureaucracy in general as well its pathologies. Chapter 2, “In Search of Normal Bureaucracy,” includes a great resource for the background of bureaucratic theory, including Weber’s ideal type, “normal” bureaucracy, and bureaucracy and structure. In Chapter 3, “Bureaucratic Pathologies and Reform,” Bozeman addresses the ills of bureaucracy, models of pathologies (which include goal ambiguity, utility maximization, property rights and principal-agent, and maladaptation), and attempts at reform, including the 1993 Government Performance and Results Act. One of the more compelling aspects of this chapter is the idea that red tape is one of many pathological aspects of bureaucracy. Bozeman cites Gerald Caiden’s (1991) list of over 175 “bureaupathologies.” Other bureaupathologies include abuse of authority, busywork, corruption, discrimination, favoritism, fraud, indifference, malfeasance, phony contracts, reluctance to take responsibility, theft, and unfairness. Bozeman includes this list to show that red tape is just one of many pathologies in a bureaucratic setting, but it is an important one we love to hate. Interestingly, two of Caiden’s bureaupathologies are delay and waste, which often are discussed in relation to red tape. Red tape is not delay, nor is it waste, according to Bozeman, who argues that red tape are essentially ineffective rules. Even to a student not at all interested in red tape, these chapters are valuable resources for understanding organization theories and bureaucracy. For the rest of the book, Bozeman explains his theory of red tape and applies it to a specific policy area. Chapter 4, “Rules and Red Tape,” introduces the reader to the theory and the “language of rules.” One critical distinction made here is that formalization and red tape are not one and the same. Formalization, defined as “the extent to which rules, procedures, instructions, and communications are written” (Pugh et al. 1968, p. 75 as cited in Bozeman 2000, p. 65), makes up the “physiology” of the organization, whereas red tape is considered pathology. Chapter 5, “Rules ‘Born Bad’: Rule-Inception Red Tape,” covers the many reasons why rules might be doomed from the start. Some rules are red tape from the get-go and Bozeman introduces five reasons for that: incorrect rule forecasts, illegitimate functions, negative sum compromise, overcontrol, and negative sum process. A key point made here is that a rule that is not red tape is not automatically a good rule. In contrast to rules born bad, Bozeman explains that rules can change and introduces six reasons that rules become red tape: rule drift, implementation change, change in the functional object, change in the rule’s ecology, rule strain, and rule incompatibility. In Chapter 6, Bozeman explains the “organizational phantom.” Organizations are likely to have rules created by “phantoms:” people who are no longer with the organization. These “phantoms pose an obvious problem and an obvious solution” (p. 107). As a result, he suggests that an organization be critical of its rules by asking “why do we do this, does anyone know?” (p. 107) and utilize his red tape audit introduced in the book’s final chapter (p. 176–81). Thus, even though red tape is pathological and perhaps inherent in any organization, there are things managers can do to reduce red tape in their organizations. At the end of Chapter 6, Bozeman presents his “Model of Red Tape Origins,” which organizes the concepts and theories into a graphical depiction (p. 119). Chapter 7, “Government Red Tape,” considers the relationship between red tape and publicness as well as the role red tape plays in governmental organizations. In Chapter 8, “Red Tape and Environmental Policy,” Bozeman, along with chapter coauthor Leisha DeHart-Davis, examines Title V of the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990 in light of red tape theory. This examination is particularly helpful as it guides the reader in what application of red tape theory might look like. Finally, in Chapter 9, “Cutting Red Tape: A Balance Model of Bureaucratic Reform,” Bozeman introduces his balance model, which blends the public management reform movement with consideration of bureaucratic pathologies, such as red tape. In other words, Bozeman (p. 167) argues that reform efforts should include considerations for efficiency, accountability, performance, and fairness, as well as resolving known organizational pathologies. Finally, Bozeman ends with the aforementioned “Red Tape Audit,” which is to help managers evaluate and eliminate red tape in their organizations. While I remember my first encounter with Bozeman’s (2000) book, I don’t exactly remember the circumstances that led me to Rosemary O’Leary’s The Ethics of Dissent: Managing Guerrilla Government —whether it was the result of my interest in whistleblowing or my interest in ethics and rule bending. I initially read the first edition (O’Leary 2006), but for this review, I include details about the second edition, released in 2014. Over time, I found this book to be valuable in solidifying my understanding about bureaucracy and dissent within it, which connects to bureaucratic rules, rule bending, and ethics, all topics I continue to study.1 Guerrilla Government is what O’Leary uses to refer to “the actions taken by career public servants who work against the wishes—either implicitly or explicitly communicated—of their superiors. …[it] is a form of dissent carried out by those who are dissatisfied with the actions of public organizations, programs, or people but who typically choose strategically not to go public with their concerns in whole or in part” (O’Leary 2014, p. xi). Thus, not all guerrillas are whistleblowers. The book’s prelude introduces examples of government guerrillas: Japanese diplomat Chiune Suighara, who helped Jews escape from Lithuania in the early 1940s; former FBI associate director Mark Felt, also known as “Deep Throat,” who assisted Washington Post reporters in uncovering the Watergate scandal in the 1970s; and Private First Class Bradley Manning, who provided Wikileaks with classified US government documents (p. 1–3). These examples are high profile but O’Leary (p. 3) argues that guerrilla government is an everyday occurrence: Sometimes guerrillas fail to correct superiors’ mistakes and let them fall. Sometimes guerrillas fail to implement orders they think are unfair. At times, guerrilla government manifests itself as the ghostwriting of letters and testimony for interest groups. At other times, it may mean forging secret links with nongovernmental organizations. At still other times, it may mean leaking information to the media. There are as many variations of guerrilla government as there are variations in guerrillas. Furthermore, O’Leary theorizes that guerrilla government occurs as the result “of inevitable tensions between bureaucracy and democracy that will never go away. These tensions yield immense ethical and management challenges as well as several harsh realities” (p. 3). Finally, she closes the prelude by advocating for organizational cultures that encourage dissent, so as to limit the necessity for government guerrilla activity. O’Leary sums up the myriad dimensions of guerrilla government quite early on (p. xi): Guerrilla government is about the power of career bureaucrats, the tensions between career bureaucrats and political appointees, the intrinsic and extrinsic motivations of public employees, organization culture, the use of the media as a public management tool, collaborative public management, networked governance, and what it means to act responsibly, ethically, and with integrity as a public servant. Chapter 1, “Guerrilla What?”, goes into more detail about these dimensions. This chapter is particularly useful for students and scholars of the three lenses through which government guerrilla can be viewed: bureaucratic politics, organizations and management, and ethics. Each of these provides perspective about guerrilla government and O’Leary does a fine job bringing together a multitude of theories and authors to support those perspectives. Here, I highlight a few I find particularly significant. The bureaucratic politics angle speaks to the tensions between bureaucracy and democracy that O’Leary addresses: bureaucrats make policy when they utilize their discretionary judgment (p. 10). Part of the explanation of guerrilla activity lies in street level bureaucracy theory: many bureaucrats have autonomy and discretion that allows them the opportunity to dissent (p. 15). This dissent is also related to rule bending: government guerrillas, in dissenting, are likely to bend rules (p. 16). The second lens through which guerrilla government can be viewed considers organizational theory. Attention here is paid to open and closed systems and networks (p. 16–7). Guerrillas often use ties with others in their policy environment to assist them in their actions. The third lens is ethics. It is worthy to note that guerrilla government is not inherently good or bad: some of these people are working for what they feel is right and consistent with what they feel their organization should be doing but isn’t, while others may be working for what they personally feel is best (p. 6). Because ethics involves right and wrong, this lens is particularly appropriate. O’Leary discusses Waldo’s 12 ethical obligations, many of which conflict with one another. A government guerrilla may be balancing his or her ethical obligations in such a way that requires them to dissent against their organization. Bookended between the first and last chapters are stories of guerrilla government. The second chapter, “Guerrilla Government and the Nevada Wetlands,” highlights the work done by the “Nevada Four” to save wetlands threatened by governmental activity. Chapter 3, “Guerrilla Government in the EPA’s Seattle Regional Office,” tells of the actions taken by staff members who fought against their superior political appointees to ensure that air quality was top priority. The story of a former Forest Service employee who fought the agency on its preservation efforts given its actions that allowed off-road vehicles in a forest is included in Chapter 4, “A Government Guerrilla Sues His Own Agency: Off-Road Vehicles in the Hoosier National Forest.” The final in-depth case study, about Bradley Manning, who illegally released a large number of American classified documents to Wikileaks, is told in Chapter 5, “Wikileaks and Guerrilla Government: The World’s Largest Security Breach.” This chapter is new to the book’s second edition. It is particularly useful in that it provides an in-depth look into guerrilla government that is not environmental in context. Tucked in between these four chapters are interludes, which include “mini-stories” of guerrilla government. In all, there is a lot upon which the reader can base their understanding of what guerrilla government looks like. O’Leary closes the book with Chapter 6, “Managing Guerrilla Government: Ethical Crusaders or Insubordinate Renegades?” Here, she introduces five “harsh realities” of guerrilla government: it is “here to stay” (p. 107); it can be done “to you in ways you’ll never know” (p. 108); it is not “all created equal” (p. 110); “[m]ost public organizations are inadequately equipped to deal effectively with” it (p. 114); and “the tensions inherent in guerrilla government will never be resolved” (p. 117). Throughout discussion of these realities, O’Leary offers practical advice. For example, box 6.1 is a list of “Guidelines for Guerrillas from Guerrillas.” On page 114, there is a list of questions that anyone who is considering guerrilla government activity can consider. On the same page, four “primary conditions” conducive to guerrilla government are listed. In response to these conditions, O’Leary considers conflict resolution as a potential solution. Importantly, O’Leary (p. 116) gleans from the literature that a “workplace climate in which disputes are constructively addressed and resolved” is one way to handle dissent that may lead to guerrilla activity if unchecked. Finally, O’Leary introduces “Advice from the Pros,” which she gathered from her interviews with public managers: “Cultivate Organization Culture” (p. 127); “Listen” (p. 128); “Understand the Formal and Informal Organization” (p. 130); “Separate the People from the Problem” (p. 131); “Create Multiple Channels for Dissent” (p. 132); and “Create Dissent Boundaries and Know When to Stop” (p. 133). Each of these is discussed in detail and can be useful for public managers, whether they currently deal with dissent and the potential government guerrilla or not. Finally, the book ends with “Postlude: Are There Lessons?” that includes questions to consider, organized by topic and chapter. Until this point, I have provided overviews of two public management books: one focusing on red tape and the other on government guerrillas. Not only are these among my favorite public administration books, they have also been instrumental in shaping my research agenda. In my dissertation (Borry 2013), I studied two “unintended consequences” of rules: rule bending and perceived red tape. Rules are in place to bring about predictable and standardized behavior across an organization, but that’s not always the outcome. Rules can be bent or broken, potentially by a government guerrilla. Rules can also be red tape, evolve into red tape, or be perceived as red tape. These books have been critical to my understanding of organizational rules and the many facets they have. t: Unconscious Bias in Citizens’ Evaluations of Public Sector Performance
abs: The premise of our article is that repeated exposure to antipublic sector messages affects the way people evaluate the performance of public sector organizations. More specifically, we argue that individuals’ implicit attitudes regarding public sector organizations are biased: Citizens automatically and unconsciously associate public sector organizations with inefficiency, inflexibility, and other pejoratives, and these automatic associations color their assessments of public sector performance. Implicit antipublic sector bias has important theoretical implications. It may help to explain whether, and to what degree, individuals respond favorably to positive public sector performance information. More specifically, it suggests that individuals’ evaluations of government performance will be weighed down by their deep-seated, unconscious views of the public sector; that the effect of information on individuals’ performance evaluations will be short-lived; and that individuals’ underlying beliefs about public sector performance will be difficult to change. We design three survey experiments to investigate these propositions, focusing on individuals’ evaluations of United States Postal Service (USPS) performance. We find evidence for each proposition.

t: Bridging Public Administration and Organizational Studies Research
abs: Looking back on my time as a PhD student, I would say that doing research was much like finding my way through uncharted waters. The starting point of my journey was to explore those articles and books that my advisors considered to be key publications. Next, I expanded my horizon by analyzing the general research streams to which this core literature belonged. It did not take long for me to identify promising niches in the literature that others seemed to have overlooked or ignored. However, as my research interests developed, I became aware that many of my “original” research ideas had already been studied, in some form or shape, in other domains. At first, I found this observation disheartening. There are few things more frustrating for a young scholar than to come up with a marvelous new research idea, only to find that the idea is neither new nor marvelous at all. Yet, I quickly realized that integrating elements from different, but related, research streams offers much potential. Scholars can apply existing insights from other disciplines to their own context, rather than reinventing the wheel. Research questions and methodologies generated by this process will be embedded more firmly in the literature, which is arguably a necessary condition for high quality research. The argument that research should not be confined to specific domains is certainly not new. Indeed, there have been fervent calls in favor of more interdisciplinary research for decades, which is a particularly relevant dynamic for relatively young research domains like public administration. I have found that The Dynamics of Rules: Change in Written Organizational Codes, by James G. March, Martin Schulz, and Xueguang Zhou, offers an excellent opportunity for such cross-fertilization, in this case between organizational studies and public administration research. Specifically, I believe that The Dynamics of Rules can make an important contribution to research on rule effectiveness in general, and organizational red tape in particular. Before discussing the contents and potential value added of The Dynamics of Rules, I will first briefly outline some of the main limitations of existing public administration research on the effectiveness of written rules. In a nutshell, written rules structure how society, organizations, and individuals are required to function or act. This line of reasoning implies that large parts of the public administration literature are concerned with written rules in one way or another. For example, a general theme underlying much research in public administration and public management is the implementation of external rules at the organizational level, and consequences thereof. However, the most notable research stream that explicitly deals with written rules in public administration research is undoubtedly red tape. Pioneered by Barry Bozeman, red tape has become a key “home grown” research topic. Since the early 1990s, red tape—which can be conceptualized as ineffective, or pathological, written organizational rules—has been studied in relation to a wide variety of other concepts that include work alienation, leadership styles, and organizational effectiveness. If we consider that empirical red tape research has only been around for roughly two decades, the existing pool of red tape studies is quite diverse and insightful. At the same time, our understanding of red tape is limited inter alia by public administration’s recurring pet peeve: an over-reliance on survey data. Unfortunately, for a stream of literature that is concerned with the effectiveness of written rules, existing red tape research has surprisingly little to do with written rules. I argue that this is where the value added of The Dynamics of Rules lies. The Dynamics of Rules is an extensive study of rule evolution at Stanford University. The authors use count data of organizational rule stocks to explain patterns of rule birth and change (which includes death) over time. The book’s focus is on theorizing about rule dynamics and carefully mapping these dynamics over time. In my view, the book’s main contribution for public administration scholars is of a methodological nature, though the theoretical expositions about the evolution of written rules are also noteworthy. For example, four images of rules are outlined in Chapter 1. The first image assumes that rules are rational efforts to organize collectivities, such as teams or coalitions. In the presence of conflicts of interest, organizational rules are introduced to curb the pursuit of self-interest. According to this view, rules are first negotiated among self-serving participants, after which individual actors attempt to maximize their wellbeing within the restrictions of the rules. The second image views rules as proliferating organisms, which reflects (post-) Weberian rule breeding processes. In this view, the enforcement of rules, unification of rule stocks, and creation of new problems by existing rules, all require additional rule-making. Third, rules can be seen as constructions of meaning. This conceptualization assumes that organizations may be judged simply by the rules they have as many certifications by external agencies are based on an audit of organizational rules. Fourth, rules are conceptualized as depositories of knowledge that evolve as a result of sequential experiences. These four images hint at different expectations about rule evolution. Whereas the rules as proliferating organisms image assumes that rule stocks will continuously increase, the constructions of meaning image implies that, in the best case scenario, rule stocks are shaped in direct response to the current environment. As a result, outdated rules would be abolished quickly and, thus, dampen rule stock growth. To determine which type of underlying processes shape rule evolution, March and colleagues use longitudinal rule count data at Stanford University. A distinction is made between two types of organizational rules: administrative rules (e.g. procedural rules related to expense reimbursement) and academic rules (e.g. requirements for degrees). The sample period runs from 1961 to 1987 for the former type of rules, and from 1891 to 1987 for the latter. Each rule has a birth date, and may have a number of revisions and a suspension date. Information on these dynamics for administrative rules is obtained from Stanford’s Administrative Guide. The primary data source for information on academic rules is the minutes from the Academic Council and Faculty Senate, but additional rule dynamics are filtered from sources such as the Faculty Handbook, Register, and Bulletin. Next, event count and history analysis (e.g. Poisson regression and hazard rate models) is used to explain rule birth (Chapter 5) and rule change (Chapter 6) patterns over time. The authors analyze and discuss a wide variety of rule dynamics drivers, but a number of findings stand out in particular. Rule births of administrative rules are partly driven by factors like increases in legislation and the number of students, but these structural and environmental effects are less pronounced for rule changes. By contrast, academic rule births and changes both appear to be more isolated from environmental pressures. As a result, the authors conclude that new rules are often created in response to external shocks, or changes in constituencies, whereas rule changes are mostly regulated by an internal historical dynamic. Overall, rule stocks at Stanford have increased over time, but at a decreasing rate. The rule count approach put forward and tested in The Dynamics of Rules thus provides a compelling narrative of quantifiable dynamics within populations of rules. Yet, many scholars have rightly pointed out that such a quantitative approach tells only part of the story. Are smaller rule stocks “better” than larger rule stocks? What share of rules has actual impact on organizations and individuals, and how many rules are essentially inactive? And what proportion of rules can be considered red tape? Indeed, it is even difficult to see to what extent the quantitative evolution of rule stocks reflects the four images of rules put forward by the authors in Chapter 1. For example, I do not believe that count analyses are an appropriate instrument to determine the extent to which rules have been created to curb self-interested behavior by individuals. Rule count studies are, by their very design, unable to answer these types of questions. Hence, we have come full circle. On the one hand, rule count studies offer an interesting and fresh perspective on analyzing general, longitudinal patterns of rule evolution, but largely ignore the specific content of rules. On the other hand, interviews and survey data limit researchers in terms of causality and generalizability. In order to effectively untangle rule dynamics, I have tried to incorporate the best of both worlds in my dissertation by combining rule count studies with survey and interview data. This approach has resulted in a wide variety of new research questions that I would like to study in the following years. Hence, I have found that interdisciplinary research not only offers theoretical and methodological synergies, but also stimulates creativity. This, I would argue, is a worthwhile outcome in and of itself.

t: Reconsidering Classic Foundations
abs: In looking back, my first years on faculty have been the whirlwind many warned it would be. The source of the whirlwind has not only been in learning to balance the many demands of research, teaching, and service, but also in finding my own approach to research and teaching. One text that has been key in helping me pave my own path, for both teaching and research, is The Oxford Handbook of Sociology and Organization Studies: Classical Foundations. How this text has been valuable as a teaching resource is probably more obvious. I have had the opportunity to teach PhD students every semester since I started on the faculty. And as is probably typical, in prepping my PhD courses I relied on the courses I had as a PhD student. In addition, though, I have used several chapters in this text as a way of incorporating some classical foundations in a way that discusses the contribution of those works as well as how those ideas are still relevant for today’s research. As Davis and Zald warn in the last chapter of The Handbook, a canon is inseparable from the historical intellectual, social, and political environment. Rather than require my own students to read the works I had to as a student, this text helped me with choosing works that I believe are important not because they are part of a canon, but because of the contribution they made to the field and how the ideas are still relevant for today’s discussions. An unforeseen benefit I had from reading the various chapters in The Handbook was that to my own research. I admit that I have always been heavily influenced by classical scholars; after all Barnard (1938) provided the framework for my dissertation on inter-organizational networks. However, in reading through several chapters of this text, I discovered or rediscovered other classical works that I found enhanced my theoretical argument in various manuscripts I was working on at the time. These two benefits that I derived from The Handbook speak to the functions of classics Stinchcombe (1982) described: as examples of excellence, as developmental tasks, as orientations to traditions, as genealogy, as a source of hypotheses, and as professional binding. Many of these functions point to the importance of the classics for teaching, but note that the function as source of hypotheses points to progressing scholarship as well. Chapter 2 of The Handbook by Thornton nicely demonstrates that particular function of the classics. In that chapter, Thornton provides three examples of influential contemporary pieces and how their use of classical works elevated their theoretical arguments. Along those lines, I approached my review of this text from that perspective. The chapters I highlight or categorize as missed opportunities are based on the contribution the authors made not so much in speaking to the contribution the classical scholar made, but how the ideas they proposed are relevant to today’s research. To be clear, The Handbook is based on a sociological perspective and the intent was to take the classic sociologists and link their contribution to one area of sociology, organization theory. Therefore, the ideal audience for this text is those who do draw on organization theory in their own research. The text is divided into two main parts. The first part focuses on European scholars and the second on American scholars. I will divide my review, however, by those chapters that were from my own perspective highlights and those that were missed opportunities. The chapters that I found especially intriguing were chapter 6 on Weber, chapter 8 on Michels, Chapter 13 on Simmel, chapter 20 on Dewey, and chapter 27 on Parsons. Two chapters were devoted to Weber, but chapter 6 by Clegg and Lounsberry provides more depth on how revisiting Weber may offer insights for the study of contemporary organizations. Clegg and Lounsberry go beyond Weber’s work on bureaucracy and instead focus on unpacking his thoughts on domination. In addition, they go beyond his three types of domination and discuss his proposed types of rationality. Clegg and Lounsberry note the opportunities to use Weber’s work on domination and rationality to connect with current research on power and authority as well as culture in understanding contemporary organizations and interorganizational relations. Chapter 8 on Robert Michels by Tolbert and Hiatt also nicely reviews Michel’s contribution and extends his argument about the nature of oligarchies in political organizations to economic organizations. Though this focus on economic organizations may be of less interest to Public Administration scholars, the connections Tolbert and Hiatt make between Michels’ argument and the research stemming from that argument, specifically Lipset et al. (1956) and Rothschild-Whitt (1979) provides insights for threads of research in Public Administration such as representative bureaucracy and public participation. Like with Weber, two chapters were also devoted to the work of Georg Simmel. Chapter 13 by Kanter and Khurana offered more insights on linkages to contemporary research than did the chapter by Scott. Both chapters noted the influence of Simmel in sociology and on network theory and attempted to extend Simmel’s contribution to organizational theory more specifically. The chapter by Kanter and Khurana succeeded more successfully by taking Simmel’s work on the types of social interactions and extending that to the implications for groups, leadership, and authority in organizations, networks, and modern society. An especially insightful chapter was chapter 20 by Cohen on John Dewey. What was especially intriguing about this chapter was how Cohen went beyond Dewey’s contribution and focused on the trajectory not taken. Cohen compares Dewey’s perspective on habit with Herbert Simon’s and how Simon led the field along a different trajectory than the path that Dewey’s perspective would have provided. Cohen makes a strong case for how revisiting Dewey’s work can make important contributions to progress the emerging study of routines and practices in organizations. Whether or not a reader is interested in pragmatism or the implications of habit in organizations, this chapter provides a concrete example of what Davis and Zald warn in the last chapter of the text, about how a canon directs us away from certain contributions at the same time that it directs us toward certain contributions. The final chapter I will highlight in a positive light is chapter 27 on Talcott Parsons by Heckscher. Though Parsons had been a very influential scholar in sociology at his time, his influence faded with the critique of his overly functional approach. Heckscher revitalizes Parsons in this chapter by making the case for how Parsons’ systems approach is valuable for business firms of today, specifically in regard to cross-functional collaboration. I was especially pleased to read this chapter as I had on my own accord come to see the value of Parsons for the study of network systems. This chapter by Heckscher offers detailed insights of how Parsons can guide research and practice on collaboration across different functions. Not all chapters in this text were highlights. Some chapters failed to convince me of the implications of known or lesser known classical scholarship on contemporary research. Some chapters are a missed opportunity. For instance, chapter 21 on Mary Parker Follet by Ansell was one of those chapters. Though Ansell provided a very nice overview of Follet and her pragmatism and the model of organization her work suggests, I desperately wanted Ansell to more explicitly link Follet’s model of organization to contemporary research. I find a great deal of potential to use Follet to further develop theory about contemporary approaches to organizing; this chapter was a missed opportunity to illuminate those possibilities. The same is true of chapter 17 on W.E.B. Dubois by Nkomo. Nkomo offers a nice overview of Dubois and the study of race. Although I was excited to read this chapter, as with Follet, there could have been a stronger link between the work of Dubois and the implications for the study of race in contemporary organizations. Perhaps, though, my disappointment in these chapters is unfair since the authors of these chapters likely had a greater task in reviewing scholars that have been overlooked in the traditional canon. The same is not true for the other chapters I found disappointing, especially those regarding Emile Durkheim and Bureaucratic Theory scholars. From my perspective, the work of Durkheim could have great contributions to current theory and research on contemporary organizations, especially as we grapple with different approaches to organizing; but Frank Dobbin’s chapter (9) did not hit upon that opportunity. In addition, two chapters (25 and 26) were devoted to the work of bureaucratic theorists, including Merton, Selznick, Gouldner, Blau and Crozier. Both of these chapters provided an overview of the contributions of these scholars, but failed to offer new insights that might be derived from this work for contemporary studies. Both Reed (chapter 25) and Haverman (chapter 26) did attempt to extend the discussion in this regard at the end of their chapters; but those discussions were limited. Finally, one cannot reflect on a text of this nature and not consider the missing chapters. Since The Handbook represents a sociological perspective, rather than critiquing the text for missing chapters, I have reviewed the text from a public management perspective noting the areas I think would be interesting to any scholar who studies organizations and management in the public domain. My hope is that texts like The Handbook and similar forthcoming texts1focus an interesting conversation around those in our field we would consider classical scholars and how their contributions might inform our current research. To do so, though, I recognize it is necessary to see value in returning to those classics. As Adler discusses in the opening chapter of the book, in the natural sciences there is danger in hesitating to forget the founders, but he argues that the danger for the social sciences is in forgetting those founders. As Adler contends, the point is not to minimize the contribution of recent scholarship, but rather that the insights of the classical scholars can inspire new theoretical and empirical research. In fact, revisiting the insights of the prominent and not so prominent scholars of our field might just be what we need to help bring more theory into our empirically sophisticated contemporary scholarship. Or perhaps not, but that is at least the approach that has helped me in finding my way in the whirlwind of my first years on faculty.

t: Bringing the Individual Back In: Interpersonal Networks in Public Administration and Management
abs: Kilduff and Krackhardt’s Interpersonal Networks in Organizations: Cognition, Personality, Dynamics, and Culture is part of the Structural Analysis in the Social Sciences series edited by Mark Granovetter. The two authors, both distinguished network scholars, wrote this book to combine and update their more than two decades of scholarship on social networks which has traversed the fields of anthropology, psychology, sociology, and management. The major contribution of this book to the study of organizations and management is their focus on network cognition and their application of methodologies that bridge psychological, sociological, and structural approaches. While networks, as theory, metaphor, and method, have become increasingly prominent in the fields of public administration and public management, the network paradigm has focused almost exclusively on interorganizational relationships. Research on policy networks, governance networks, and service delivery networks emphasize the formal and informal ties that emerge among organizational level actors. Much less attention has been given to the interpersonal networks that form within public and nonprofit organizations. Organization and management scholars have long stressed the importance of interpersonal relations for both individual and collective performance. The instrumental and affective relations linking employees together are seen as the pathways by which information and knowledge are exchanged and emotional support offered. In Herbert Simon’s classic text, Administrative Behavior, he defined an organization as a “complex pattern of communication and relationships in a group of human beings” (1997, p. 19). Simon urged scholars to take a rigorous methodological approach, aligned with social psychology and the broader field of organization studies, in their analysis of public organizations and decision-making. However, as noted by Kelman (2007), Simon’s call, and his departure from our field, was the “road not taken” for scholars of public administration. Kilduff and Krackhardt’s book provide us with a roadmap to follow the path outlined by Simon more than 60 years ago. For researchers in public administration and public management, Interpersonal Networks in Organizations offers three primary means for advancing scholarship by emphasizing social context, bridging micro and macro perspectives, and exploring cognitive social structures. First, the authors move organizational research beyond its traditional focus on microlevel attitudes to embrace the social context in which those attitudes form. Traditional research on topics ranging from employee commitment to employee performance has focused on variables that exist at the individual or organizational level. Given that an organization is a “pattern of communication and relationships”, is it likely that individual attitudes and behaviors in the workplace do not develop independently but rather are socially constructed. Indeed, evidence dating back to the Hawthorne studies suggests as much. However, rigorous statistical analyses assessing the role of social context and interpersonal relations on individual beliefs and behaviors are generally missing from mainstream public administration research. Second, while Interpersonal Networks in Organizations concerns social structures, it is very much focused on “bringing the individual back in” when conducting organizational network studies. To this end, the authors bridge micro and macro perspectives on longstanding organizational issues. Their approach, termed cognitive social network research “explores topics related to the dynamic interplay of distinctive individuals in complex social networks in organizations” (p. 259). While the extant network literature has identified the benefits that accrue to individuals for occupying certain structural positions, such as structural holes, research remains limited on how or why certain individuals are able to better navigate the social milieu of their organizations to obtain these structurally advantageous positions. Furthermore, little is known about how and why certain individuals are able to differentially capitalize on their structural positions to create tangible benefits. Kilduff and Krackhardt highlight how individual traits and cognitions shape the types of networks one builds and the types of benefits one receives. Third, the authors demonstrate the importance of network perceptions, something they refer to as cognitive social structures. Anyone who has worked for an organization understands the need to assess the social context of their job environment. When we arrive at a new place of employment we immediately begin to develop perceptions of the social landscape and of the individuals we need to interact with to acquire necessary information and accomplish work goals. The process of scanning the social structure is as much instinctive as it is strategic. Kilduff and Krackhardt demonstrate that individual ability to understand social contexts varies considerably and differences in the accuracy by which one can assess an organization’s social structure has implications for leadership, performance, and power. Thus, rather than viewing a network as a singular entity, the authors provide an approach to measure individual perceptions of social structure and use those perceptions to identify the “real” network. The book consists of twelve chapters and three sections: (a) Perceiving Networks, (b) The Psychology of Network Differences, and (c) Network Dynamics and Organizational Culture. In the first section on network perceptions, the authors explore the schemas and heuristics used by employees to develop perceptions of the social networks that surround them. The authors demonstrate that power and leadership capacity are affected by the accuracy of one’s perception of the network. In other words, “Cognitive accuracy of the informal network is, in and of itself, a base of power” (p. 85). They also explore the relative importance of perceived network ties versus actual network ties. They find that peer perceptions of relations with prominent members of the organization were stronger predictors of performance reputation than the actual existence of the relationship. The second section on “The Psychology of Network Differences” demonstrates how network behavior and outcomes are strongly influenced by differences in personality. Unlike a strict structural approach, which emphasizes network position (often ignoring individual differences), the authors explore the interdependencies between personality traits and social networks. In this section, questions ranging from why certain individuals are more susceptible to peer influence and how performance in an organization is a product of self-monitoring behavior and network structure are explored. The final section, “Network Dynamics and Organizational Culture”, consists of three chapters examining organizational turnover, crisis, and culture. In the chapter on organizational crisis the authors argue that “emergent networks, left to themselves without the aid of conscious design, will form naturally in ways that are suboptimal, even dysfunctional, for the organization.” As with their previous findings, the results suggest the need for managers to attend to the informal networks in their organization. With regard to turnover, Kilduff and Krackhardt provide evidence to suggest that one’s decision to leave an organization is not driven simply by individual attributes but rather occurs in patterns and clusters linked to the social networks within the organization. The areas in which Interpersonal Networks in Organizations is relevant for current research in public administration and public management are vast. The following are a few of the areas that I see as the most exciting. The first is individual and collective performance. While the provision of government services often occurs through interorganizational arrangements, single organizations are still responsible for specific functions: educating school children, providing healthcare, housing inmates etc. The ever evolving and complex demands placed on public employees to carry out these functions require them to be continuous learners and rely on their peers to reduce uncertainty. Because sensemaking and knowledge exchange are relational processes, the interpersonal networks that emerge are critical components in determining the effectiveness of public agencies. Future research on the creation of public value and organizational performance should consider both the broader interorganizational networks an agency is embedded in as well as the interpersonal networks that exist within the agency. Recent advances in statistical network models allow for the analysis of multilevel networks and these tools appear to be particularly relevant for our understanding of individual, organizational, and interorganizational performance. Second, as performance measures become common mechanisms of accountability and efficiency, understanding how the social environment of an organization shapes these measures is critical. Many public organizations have implemented some form of a merit pay program; a policy that is increasingly prominent in the public school system. Under merit pay programs, individual performance is measured and used to determine one’s salary and even one’s continued employment in the organization. Inherent in the idea of merit pay is the notion that individuals are in control of their level of performance. To some extent this is true, but increasingly research suggests that social structures also shape performance. For example, work by Pil and Leana (2009) found that a one standard deviation increase in tie strength among teachers increased their students performance by 5.7%. Therefore, some teachers, simply by being placed in more densely connected schools or on certain grade level teams, are more likely to be higher performers than an equally skilled peer in another context. This creates a fundamental problem for measuring and rewarding individual outcomes. Furthermore, by stressing individual goals, organizations may witness negative implications on interpersonal relations as employee propensity to collaborate and exchange information is reduced. Third, Interpersonal Networks in Organizations illustrates new types of variables and methodological approaches to the study of traditional concepts like public service motivation, organizational commitment, and turnover. Kilduff and Krackhardt provide tools and theories to more clearly assess how individual beliefs and behaviors are socially constructed. An emphasis on the role of cognition and networks sheds light on the social processes often hidden in organizations that may ultimately shape employee motivation, retention, and organizational culture. Given that beliefs and behaviors are partly products of interpersonal relations, these findings have important implications for how public organizations structure work teams, hire and promote employees, and engage in reform efforts. Overall, there are fascinating findings, ideas, and methods throughout this book that offer insights into the ways that public administration and management scholars could expand and deepen their research agendas.

t: The Starting Point for Nonprofit Scholarship
abs: The first year on the job as an assistant professor is a period of adjustment, the start of not just a job but a career, almost always in a new location. Piled upon these major changes are minor ones: fitting yourself and family into a new environment, preparing new classes, shifting from dissertation writing to stand alone publications, finding one’s place among new colleagues, advising more than being advised, and even unpacking and decorating a new office in the fruitless attempt to fill the bookshelves and walls. Throughout such tumultuous times, dependable sources of information and wisdom are essential. Friends and colleagues occupy most of these roles, but even a book can have a place. In my first year on the job, The Nonprofit Sector: A Research Handbook, Second Edition edited by Walter W. Powell and Richard Steinberg (2006), filled such a role. A key resource in the development of my dissertation research as a graduate student, this book met an even broader set of purposes during the start of my academic career.

t: The Importance of Ethical Leadership and Personal Control in Promoting Improvement-Centered Voice among Government Employees
abs: The purpose of this article is to provide insight about the conditions in which government employees are more likely to engage in voice to improve performance of their organization. In this effort, the current research examines the direct and interactive effects of ethical leadership and perceptions of personal control on improvement-centered voice among government employees. These relationships are examined with data that were collected through two separate surveys from 477 employees and 161 managers working in a large state agency. The results indicate that ethical leadership and personal control, after controlling for employee characteristics, job satisfaction, procedural fairness, and performance monitoring, are related positively with supervisor ratings of subordinate voice behavior. The results also show that the effect of ethical leadership on voice becomes significantly stronger when employees perceive that they have higher levels of discretion over work behaviors and influence on decisions in their workgroup. Implications of these findings for research and practice are discussed.

t: Stakeholders in the Same Bed with Different Dreams: Semantic Network Analysis of Issue Interpretation in Risk Policy Related to Mad Cow Disease
abs: The “Risk Society” as Ulrich Beck (Beck, Ulrich. 1992. Risk society: Towards a new modernity. London, UK: Sage, Beck, Ulrich. 1999. World risk society. Cambridge, UK: Polity Press) has called modern society, has changed the policy dynamics of many high-risk policies. Policy conflicts occur due to both physically objective risks and socially constructed risks. Risk politicization means that issue expansion and attention cycles are likely to be related to the social construction of policy images. An interesting case in point concerns the risk perception about Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) among four groups of people in South Korea: bureaucrats, citizens, scientists, and interest groups. We develop expectations about how the four groups will frame the political issues based on their roles and concerns in the policy process. Downs’ (Downs, Anthony. 1972. Up and down with ecology: The issue-attention cycle. Public Interest 28:38–50) work on the issue-attention cycle suggests how issues rise and fall on the public agenda, and our work also directly tests his theses. This study uses semantic network analysis based on content analysis of key words in 6400 articles published in 2008 to construct semantic networks for the four stakeholder groups over four stages in the policy process. Through this unique data analysis, we can see the major issue concerns and intensity of each of the four groups in the four policy stages by assessing the key words each group uses in the media articles and the visualizations of their semantic associations. We do find distinct differences in what issues each of the four groups focus on and how the focus of substance changes in each of the four policy stages that clarify how these groups framed the BSE policy issues. Our results both confirm and raise doubts about some predictions from the issue-attention cycle. Citizens’ attention follows closely to Downs’ predictions, whereas the other stakeholders’ issue-attention cycles do not follow Downs’ predictions as well. Finally, our study explains and demonstrates the value of semantic network analysis as a powerful method for understanding issue framing in the policy process.

t: Coping During Public Service Delivery: A Conceptualization and Systematic Review of the Literature
abs: Frontline workers, such as teachers and social workers, often experience stress when delivering public services to clients, for instance because of high workloads. They adapt by coping, using such practices as breaking or bending rules for clients, or rationing services. Although coping is recognized as an important response to the problems of frontline work, the public administration field lacks a comprehensive view of coping. The first contribution of this article is therefore theoretical: conceptualizing coping during public service delivery and developing a coherent classification of coping. This is done via a systematic review of the literature from 1981 to 2014. The second contribution is empirical: via a systematic review of the literature from 1981–2014 this article provides a framework and analytical account of how coping during public service delivery has been studied since 1980. It highlights the importance of the type of profession (such as being a teacher or a police officer), the amount of workload, and the degree of discretion for understanding how frontline workers cope with stress. It also reveals that frontline workers often draw on the coping family “moving towards clients” revealing a strong tendency to provide meaningful public service to clients, even under stressful conditions. We conclude with an agenda for future studies, examining new theoretical, methodological and empirical opportunities to advance understanding of coping during public service delivery. Trabalhadores de linha de frente, tais como professores e assistentes sociais, frequentemente experimentam estresse no exercício de suas funções de entrega de serviços públicos para os clientes em função do acúmulo de trabalho. Eles se adaptam ao enfrentamento utilizando práticas tais como quebrar ou contornar regras para os clientes, ou racionamento de serviços. Apesar do enfrentamento ser reconhecido como uma importante resposta aos problemas de linha de frente, a administração pública se ressente de uma visão totalizadora do mesmo. A primeira contribuição do artigo é, desta forma, teórica: conceituando o enfrentamento durante a prestação de serviços públicos e o desenvolvimento de uma classificação coerente de enfrentamento. Isto é realizado via revisão sistemática da literatura de 1981 a 2014. A segunda contribuição é empírica: através de uma revisão sistemática da literatura de 1981-2014, o artigo apresenta um quadro e uma narrativa analítica de como o enfrentamento durante a prestação de serviços públicos tem sido estudada desde 1980. O texto realça a importância dos tipos de profissão (tal como ser um professor ou um agente policial), a quantidade de carga de trabalho e o grau de discernimento para o entendimento de como trabalhadores de linha de frente lidam com o estresse. Ele também revela que trabalhadores de linha de frente frequentemente recorrem à famílias de “clientes proativos” revelando uma forte tendência a entregar serviços públicos significativos para os clientes mesmo que em condições de estresse. Nós concluímos com uma agenda para estudos futuros, examinando novas teorias, métodos e oportunidades empíricas para avançar o entendimento do enfrentamento durante prestação de serviços públicos. Translated by Ricardo Gomes, University of Brasília

t: Performance Gaps and Managerial Decisions: A Bayesian Decision Theory of Managerial Action
abs: An extensive literature finds that managerial decisions matter for the performance of public organizations, yet little attention has been devoted to why managers make the decisions that they do. This article builds a theory of public management decision making based on the simple assumption that managers are concerned with performance and the performance gaps of their organization. Using a logic borrowed from bounded rationality and Bayesian decision theory, we theorize a set of prior expectations. Whether the organization meets these expectations or fails to do so is then used to specify a series of precise hypotheses about when managers make a variety of decisions including when to seek additional information, take risks, decentralize the organization, determine goals, or select a managerial strategy as well as other managerial actions. The logic of the theory can easily be extended to decisions about selecting goals or managerial strategy. We then extend the basic theory by considering multiple goals, hierarchy, and alternative theoretical approaches. Uma literatura extensa sugere que decisões gerenciais são importantes para o desempenho de organizações públicas ainda que pouca atenção tenha sido dedicada a entender por que os gerentes tomam as decisões que eles tomam. O artigo constrói uma teoria de tomada de decisão em organizações públicas baseada na simples suposição de que os gerentes estão preocupados com o desempenho e com as quedas de desempenho de suas organizações. Utilizando a lógica tomada emprestado da racionalidade limitada e da teoria de decisão Bayesiana, nós teorizamos um conjunto de expectativas prévias. Se a organização atinge ou falha em suas expectativas, isto é então utilizado para especificar uma série de hipóteses precisas sobre quando gerentes tomam uma variedade de decisões, incluindo quando procurar por informações adicionais, correr riscos, descentralizar a organização, definir metas, ou selecionar uma estratégia gerencial bem como outras ações gerenciais. A lógica da teoria pode ser facilmente estendida para decisões sobre a seleção de objetivos ou de estratégias gerenciais. Nós, então, ampliamos a base teórica considerando objetivos múltiplos, hierarquia e abordagens teóricas alternativas. Translated by Ricardo Gomes, University of Brasília
